rows.title: Manx shearwater
rows.evidence: The Manx shearwater article says the current English name refers to the nesting of this species on the Calf of Man, so the bird is named for this island.
rows.summary: The current English name was first recorded in 1835 and refers to the nesting of this species on the Calf of Man. The Manx shearwater (Puffinus puffinus) is a medium-sized shearwater in the seabird family Procellariidae.

rows.title: Northern gannet
rows.evidence: The northern gannet article says the specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth, so the species is named for this island. The colony-size sentences are not used.
rows.summary: The specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth. The northern gannet (Morus bassanus) is a seabird, the largest species of the gannet family, Sulidae.

rows.title: Glanville fritillary
rows.evidence: The article says the Glanville fritillary is a highly restricted species within the UK, confined to the Isle of Wight. The following sentence notes the Channel Islands and an introduced site on the Hampshire coast.
rows.summary: The Glanville fritillary is a highly restricted species within the UK, being confined to the Isle of Wight and even there being largely limited to the southern coast. The Glanville fritillary (Melitaea cinxia) is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It also occurs in the Channel Islands, and since 1990 there has been a mainland site on the Hampshire coast, possibly the result of an introduction.

rows.title: Red-necked phalarope
rows.evidence: The Fetlar article says the Loch of Funzie is the most important breeding site in the United Kingdom for red-necked phalaropes. The sentence has no count. The species page's 'most reliable place' sentence is visit advice and is not used.
rows.summary: Of greatest importance are red-necked phalaropes, for which the Loch of Funzie is the most important breeding site in the United Kingdom, and for a while during the 1990s was the only breeding site in the country. Fetlar is one of the North Isles of Shetland, Scotland, with a usually resident population of 61 at the time of the 2011 census and 66 in 2022.

rows.title: Atlantic puffin
rows.evidence: The Isle of May article says the island is home to one of the largest puffin colonies in the United Kingdom. Later sentences that give a seabird total or say how to reach the island are not used.
rows.summary: The island is home to one of the largest puffin colonies in the United Kingdom. The Isle of May is located in the north of the outer Firth of Forth, approximately eight kilometres (4+1⁄2 nautical miles) off the coast of mainland Scotland.

rows.title: St Kilda house mouse
rows.evidence: The article says the St Kilda house mouse is an extinct subspecies found only on the St Kilda archipelago, and it names the St Kilda field mouse as a different subspecies that is still present.
rows.summary: The St Kilda house mouse (Mus musculus muralis) is an extinct subspecies of the house mouse found only on the islands of the St Kilda archipelago of northwest Scotland. They were first described, alongside the St Kilda field mouse, by natural historian Gerald Edwin Hamilton Barrett-Hamilton in 1899. When the last St Kildans were evacuated in 1930, the endemic house mouse became extinct very quickly, as it was associated strictly with human settlement. The St Kilda field mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus hirtensis), a subspecies of the wood mouse, is still present.
